utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that the parties have some matters to raise. Who's first? Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess I can begin. I may be the only one with preliminary matters today, Your Honour. I just wanted to report back on several matters. First of all, we did file the two filings yesterday that Your Honour had suggested, so you ought to now have those so you can have the full picture and ability to see what I was laying out in court yesterday. I have spoken with both of the witnesses who were scheduled for this week and have obtained the precise details of why they're unavailable. The first, who is an attorney in Belgrade, is engaged on a trial that he thought he could try to continue but he did not obtain a continuance and therefore is engaged as an attorney rendering his professional services in another trial that is ongoing this week. The other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's engaged in a trial. He tried to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Continue the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- obtain a postponement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He wasn't successful. When he was -- when he was asked to be a witness, I mean, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was not. I was not, Your Honour. I was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then, you should have. I mean, if he's an attorney, and he's going to be a witness, I mean, why would you put him down to testify without finding out about his availability? Is this the first time that you're learning that he would be engaged in another trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Attorneys have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because that's not proper management.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Attorneys do have trials all the time, Your Honour. But with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but when you put him down first as a witness for this week, that should have been an inquiry. Are you free to testify in the trial on such and such a date? The attorney says yes, so that that must mean that he's not engaged in another trial, you know. So it leads me to wonder whether this is something new, you know, whether he wasn't aware from the very beginning that he was engaged in a trial or whether he's simply disrespectful of these proceedings. That would not be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, attorneys have trials all the time. In my jurisdiction where I come from, and I know you don't want to hear about jurisdictions, but have you to understand real life. These proceedings are not taking place outside of real life. Witnesses have lives. Witnesses have professional obligations. Things change. The schedule changes very frequently. With the time-frame that we have in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, you see, you have not given me the proper explanation. What I'm saying to you is that when you put him down as a witness to appear in this trial on a particular date, I take it to mean that he was free, but you have not said to me that since that time, some commitment has arisen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we have to file things for this court, we have to do them by the Thursday. I remind you again that we had a week, approximately, between the filing of the 65 ter and the filing of the witnesses for this week. During that week, my client tried to contact one of our witnesses to see if he was available. The Prosecution then issued a Rule 64 warning, and he was not allowed to call anyone apart from myself here in the Hague, to talk with anyone for almost a full week. He had to go on a hunger strike to try and get his rights back. We finally got his rights back, and now we ask you, who can he call to find out whether they're available? Because people are intimidating our witnesses on the ground, so they have to have contact with him to know that the people that are contacting them are legitimate people. I was supposed to go on the terrain, as I mentioned yesterday. I can't do that with this -- under this atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't make wild allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of intimidation. If you have -- that's a serious allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's a serious allegation, and it's based upon facts that I have, facts that I've talked with people. We have intimidation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you have the facts, bring them to the Court, bring them to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The other witness, that was the individual from Austria. He just started working for a leasing company and during the probationary employment period he cannot take days off with less than several weeks' notice. He had one week notice between the time-frame when we sent him the filing and said that we were listing him as a witness for these proceedings. And again, these were the two witnesses that we believed we could file because we knew that they had passports, we knew they had come to The Hague previously and were not of the witnesses that we might have to strike from the list to meet the Court's compliance with the 45 witnesses quota that was given to us, but again, these are all factors that occur in a trial, that occur in a trial that is not happening in a vacuum. You have to take things into account. You have to take the outside world into account, people's personal lives, people's professional lives --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by outside factors outside of their control. This last week was completely outside of our control. We did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, the same question would arise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down. It's really impossible to interpret. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The same question would arise as to whether when this witness was put down as a witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We thought he could attend and he thought he could attend. When he went to his employer, he found out that he could not take days off. That's the problem with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's an inquiry that should have been made before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, but the time -- you're not taking, I think, proper account of the time period involved, Your Honour, with all the other things that we had to do during the short time period that we had for this case. We had to put together the 65 ter list. We had to start responding to the allegations of the Prosecution on various levels. I've been doing e-mails --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... basic information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation will cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologize. I'm getting emotional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't get too excited.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just saying that in the ordinary course of events, that would be the first inquiry to make of a witness who is employed, whether his employer will allow him to attend court. That's the first inquiry to be made. But I just want to let you know that I know that there are difficulties in obtaining witnesses. I worked as a Crown counsel in my country, and I had problems with judges, and I can tell you a very short story that in Jamaica Crown counsel was always blamed for the absence of witnesses, and there's this particular judge, who was very, very stern. Trial was set to start. Prosecution witness is not available. And as usual, the judge turned on Crown counsel and said, Mr. Brown, where are the witnesses? This Crown counsel who was actually from Barbados, not Jamaica, said, My Lord, when I woke up this morning and turned in my bed, I did not see any of them. So I'm very familiar with the problems relating to procuring witnesses, but witnesses must appreciate that this is an international tribunal established by the United Nations. It is not a social club.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And when they are scheduled to attend, they have an obligation to attend, and they will only be excused if good cause is shown, and the last sanction which the Trial Chamber has and which will only be used as a very last measure, if there is no good cause for the witness to attend, is that that witness's time can be counted against the time allocated to the Defence and the number of witnesses. So you must always have a good cause for a witness not showing up. We will show you the same consideration, give you the same leniency that we gave the Prosecution, but it is not a good start --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- that your first two witnesses are unavailable, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, and I hope that once we have time to go out on a train, meet with these people, then we will -- once we get started, we will have a larger group of witnesses to choose from for a week; and therefore, if one is unavailable, we can move them to the end of the week, put another one forward, et cetera. Once we have a larger pool of witnesses to work with in a given week, then I think a lot of these problems with dissipate. The main problem is we only have these two witnesses that we were able to put down for this week and both of them are unavailable. To also give more information about the last matter that I had for today, I talked with Mr. Alarid yesterday and then I did also verify his plane ticket here, and I misread it yesterday. He's actually returning on the morning of Thursday, December the 4th, at 11.40 a.m., although the flight does leave the 3rd of December, I had misread it as saying he was coming here the evening of the 3rd, but it's actually the 4th when he's arriving, Your Honours, and that's a matter that I know I need to give to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And therefore he will not be available to make his opening?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would I be wrong in concluding, Mr. Ivetic, that the Defence worked on the assumption that Mr. Cepic's case would take the entire four weeks and, therefore, they were just -- you're just getting yourself ready to begin on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, we foresaw that it might start this week. I don't think we thought it was going to be undertaken in two days. Your Honour said four weeks. I think you meant four days, but we prepared for that, but again, we had so many things to do. I -- for one, I can tell you I was in gaol every day last week dealing with Mr. Lukic and trying to resolve the issue with the secretariat and trying to find out how we can put witnesses on the list. We finally put witnesses on the list. Now we've been working on trying to comply with the Court's order to try and streamline the case as much as possible without impinging upon Mr. Lukic's rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can't answer this, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I just did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- I mean, I still wonder how responsible it was for Mr. Alarid to schedule his arrival here on Thursday morning when the direction given by the Chamber made it plain that he should be ready to start immediately following the closing of the case for Mr. Lukic, Mr. Cepic's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours, always in a trial, when it's a rolling date to say when another party finishes, which is beyond our control, we have to guess at that, and sometimes we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, but if you understood that order, the language is quite plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Clearly there was a possibility that Mr. Cepic would close his case sometime before Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And our time here is very important. We can't waste it, and that is why the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- instructed that you should be ready to begin your case so soon as Mr. Cepic closes, whether that was Tuesday or Wednesday or Thursday, you should be ready, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And every other judge that Mr. Alarid is appearing in front of in New Mexico has the same attitude, that he has to be preparing cases. So his schedule ask such that he had to go back and he had meet with the witnesses, he met with some expert witnesses of ours that we have on the list, that were -- two, I think, have been approved by the registry. The others we're preparing applications for them to be approved on. He's doing work, Your Honour. He's doing work. He's not on vacation. That's -- I don't want to make any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but this work is paramount, and a counsel who appears here must accept that. He either accepts that or he doesn't. If he doesn't accept it, then he shouldn't be working here. What is the next matter, Mr. Cepic? Yes, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DER WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I have another question. I'm sorry. You were saying, once we get started, then we can put on speed, but when are you going to get started because it seems that you have not started yet, that you can't start this week. Are you going to -- is that then a moment we expect next week or when are you going to get started?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, I indicated that I did not get started because I could not move anywhere from The Hague last week, so I could not go on the train to meet with witnesses and obtain their passports, to submit them to the VWS for visas, to work with them on statements for the ones that have statements, to prepare them to testify, the job that a lawyer's supposed to do in this Tribunal. We're not supposed to bring witnesses that we've never met before, Your Honour, and because of the Prosecution's actions last week, we were unable to do that. Hopefully if we have some time I can go on the weekend and meet with four or five witnesses and have four or five witnesses for a week and then have a continuing process. That's the way Defence teams work. You have counsel, Defence counsel, interchanging roles, running out on to trains to do things. That's the way we do them. I'm well aware of that. I've been here for a number of years, and I just finished a trial that lasted two and a half years, so that's what we do, and that's what we were unable to do last week because of all the factors that we've discussed. And again, I can't stress hard enough how -- what a unique situation it was to have a client on hunger strike and having the Prosecution object to a witness that he was contacting, that they knew was one of our witnesses, that they even said, You can contact him. I -- Mr. Groome in the transcript is recorded as saying, You can contact him, and then they object to it and we're not allowed to contact anyone. It's a situation that caused a great deal of turmoil for us and made us unable to prepare our case for this week. We had hoped to present two witnesses that we could prepare under that time period, and now I'm meeting -- basically, I'm -- basically, I made a mistake by putting those two witnesses on is -- is what I'm getting. That I should have had no witnesses on the list because these witnesses are unavailable now, so it's the same as if I had no witnesses on the list. But again, if I have time, a weekend or -- if Mr. Cepic's case finishes early and we don't have trial proceedings then I can go right away and then I can witnesses, a group of witnesses for a week put together so that I can have a pool to work from to say, okay, I have five or six witnesses that are available, that have been notified to the Prosecution by the Thursday before, because of course we have that obligation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You'll be ready for Monday? I think that's the question the Judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope to be for -- with something, but I don't know at this point in time, Your Honour, until I go out into the field. I hope to have some witnesses, yes, but it all depends on a lot of things and don't forget that it depends a lot on how fast the witnesses go, too. We might have witnesses for part of the week but not the whole week. I don't know ir as we stand right now. We haven't even decided what witnesses I'm going to try and contact and get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Monday's the holiday. It's Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Tuesday. That's the goal. I mean, obviously it's always the goal to try and fill as much of the court time as possible with live witnesses or with witnesses appearing by written statement pursuant to 92 ter and 92 bis. That is the goal. That is the goal that we have as Defence counsel, but we have all these other things working against us, Your Honours, and that's what you have to take into account, and that's what I'm presenting to you, and that's all I can do. That's all I can do is present these things to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's only complaints that I've heard from you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DER WYNGAERT
utterances.text: We are Tuesday now and you don't seem to have an idea about what the witnesses are that you are going to bring next week, or am I misunderstanding you? Will you by Thursday of this week be able to produce a list?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By Thursday of this week I have to produce a list, correct, so then I will have a better idea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, since it seems that I'm being blamed for much of these problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I need to place a few things on the record. On the 18th of November -- well, it seems that I'm being accused of impeding the ability of Mr. Ivetic to contact the witness, and I flatly and categorically deny anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't know that you had that power.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't have that power, and it's being attributed to me under misrepresentations, and I had nothing to do with the timing of this. On the 18th, the registrar, the deputy registrar contacted me through a letter that was sent to counsel, I believe they knew this before I did, informing me that Mr. Lukic had called the father of Zehra Turjacanin pretending to be someone he wasn't, pretending to be in Italy rather than in the detention unit, and seeking contact information about his son. This frightened the man. Alarms were raised with registry, and both Defence counsel and I were notified about it. Three hours after I received that letter, I filed a request freezing the non-privileged phone calls of Mr. Lukic until the matter could be investigated. At that stage, I did not have the translations of the transcript of that telephone conversation. At no time was the privileged communication between Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Lukic interrupted, so I really fail to see how Mr. Ivetic claims that he was unable to be in communication with his client outside of The Hague. At any time Mr. Ivetic wanted to contact any witness, whether they were witnesses that had some relation to a Prosecution witness or not, if he had that information, he was free to do that. He did not have to go through me. Yesterday, and I think an allusion was made to it today, that this occasioned an awful lot of work on the part of the Defence team, I would point out that the appeal of that procedure was made by Mr. Lukic himself in a letter by himself. There were no filings related to this -- to my action, that letter, that were filed by either Mr. Ivetic or Mr. Alarid. It was solely done by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't want to have to carry this thing on too long. Do you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour. Yes, I do, Your Honour, because again, Mr. Groome is presenting thing that are not true. He knows very well that I sent a cease and desist notice of several pages and I had to meet with Mr. Alarid to discuss that. He knows these things. He also ought to know that the only privileged communications that Mr. Lukic can have are to the office here in The Hague. I stress that again. These actions completely disrupted any ability to go out into the terrain and do anything with witnesses, anything at all, and it's something that if he doesn't know, now he should now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think I've heard enough, Mr. Groome. I think I've heard enough, thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Our next witness. Good morning, Your Honours. Our next witness is Mr. Branimir Bugarski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a couple of preliminary matters. It will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think I'll be finished by the time the witness is brought into the courtroom. Your Honours, last evening at 9.55 p.m., I received a proofing note with respect to Mr. Bugarski, and I certainly understand that when working with witnesses they inevitably provide additional information just prior to appearing in court. I want to place on the record in light of the many objections raised during the Prosecution case regarding our supplying of proofing notes that for each of the witnesses in the Sredoje Lukic case, the Prosecution received proofing notes shortly before their testimony. The second matter, Your Honour, that I'd like to raise has to do with these documents authored by a priest in Krtinska, and my question that I seek clarification from Mr. Cepic is, we've received two different translations, two versions of translations of the document, one in which the feast day is alleged to be just an ordinary feast day and another one in which the feast day is alleged to be the village feast day of Krtinska. It seems to be an important issue. I didn't object to the priest not being here to introduce the document, but perhaps Mr. Cepic can clarify it, why there are two different translations of the same document with that -- what seems to be an important difference, and maybe put my concerns at ease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that document is already admitted. Firstly, we received that document, the last document from the local priest on 18th of November, just one day, actually on 17th of November, just one day before our 65 ter submissions, so we just have a draft translation, and later on we requested an official translation from ICTY translation service. So the new translation is from official service of this court, so that is the difference, and this new translation, official translation, is in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that's the one that should be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I simply ask, then, is it the Defence theory that the feast of the Holy Trinity is the village feast day of Krtinska or is simply just an ordinary feast day in the Serbian Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Groome could find if answer in yesterday's testimony of Mr. Zivkovic and in admitted exhibit. Thank you. And I think that it is not the moment for final arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. I agree, yes. Don't answer it. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's simply for me to know how to question these witnesses. I don't know what the theory is. I've been presented with contradictory translations of the same document. I'd like not to have to object and ask that the priest be called to explain it, but I mean, is the theory of the Defence that it is a village feast day or is it not, or -- I mean, why are we receiving contradictory information on what seems to be an issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not for you to ask. If the Chamber wishes, we will ask for the matter to be clarified. For the moment, do you have any other matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Cepic kindly speak closer to the microphone. He is barely audible to the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit, and you may begin, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bugarski.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For the record, please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Branimir Bugarski.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, would you give me the place and date of your birth.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: 19th of October, 1950.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system document number ID number 2D05-0272. That is the version in B/C/S, and the English version is 2D04-0109, please. And in the meantime, could the court usher pass this hard copy of the witness statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bugarski, did you give in January 2008 a written statement to Mr. Sredoje Lukic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you on the 1st December meeting, yesterday's meeting, with Defence team sought to alter some of the things in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You have this written statement in front of you. Did you, with respect to the last sentence in the seventh paragraph, which reads: "Milojko's son Dejan was also present there and they explained to me what happened ..." Did you want to explain who explained what?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who explained this to you.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Milojko Popadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And with respect to paragraph 9, the sentence: "We had agreed earlier that I would prepare food for them, pork, to be precise, so that they could put it in a freezer and bring it to their family in Visegrad." Did you want to explain more precisely who contacted you and who sought the pork?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the last sentence of paragraph 9: "After this conversation, they got into their vehicle and left Obrenovac." Did you want to state what you were told by them to the effect that they did not say precisely where they went but they had to go there? Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bugarski, if I were to ask you the same questions, apart from the alterations that you just stated, same questions when I interviewed you during you giving the statements, would you provide the same answers here today as you did on that other occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... statement as evidence with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask admission of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, yes. I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 2D47, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system document ID number 2D03-0266, in English is 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bugarski, who signed this certificate?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not asking you about the witness statement. Take a look at this screen. I'm sorry. I didn't instruct you to do so. Do you see a document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you see who signed it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: This certificate was signed by our pastor, priest, Petar Paraklis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who is he? What is he the pastor of?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: He's from Urovci-Krtinska parish, and he's the priest in my village, Krtinska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bugarski, it is seen here that your local priest certified that all the households celebrate the village feast day of Pentecost, the Trinity, the Most Holy Trinity.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, are these celebrations individual or for the whole village?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Holy Trinity is the village feast.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I kindly ask for admission of this exhibit, and I see that Mr. Groome is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear who Mr. Bugarski is. Did you have that already?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What work does he do, Mr. Bugarski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I being asked this question? May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a salesman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And do you know the priest -- do you know the priest, Mr. Paraklis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what kind of priest is he? Of what church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's a priest of the Orthodox church. He came there. He built an Orthodox church there -- well, he managed, and two villages of Krtinska and Urovac [as interpreted] for the services of those two villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that I may clarify the confusion which --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Inaudible. Please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So it is the wrong translation. So I would ask the witness to read the certificate in B/C/S. I found mistake now, and I apologize now for this omission from my Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're asking him to read it in B/C/S so we can have it translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bugarski, because of mistranslation, could you please read this certificate in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Certificate: Issued pursuant to the request of Mr. Branko Bugarski from Krtinska, Dorcula 65, Obrenovac municipality. Village of Krtinska, which belongs to the Urovci-Krtinska parish, in it all the household heads celebrate the descent of the host Holy Trinity, and the household head, stated above, also celebrates the Patron Saint's Day of the St. Stephen of Decani. The parish hereby confirms and certifies that the above is accurate, certified by the Urovci-Krtinska parish priest, Petar Paraklis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bugarski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Whose statement is this? Is it the statement of this witness or of the priest?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: From the priest. He just read the -- he just read this certificate from the priest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is the priest's certificate. Is he available, the priest?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I can contact him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He would be the best person to give this evidence, it would seem to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DER WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, may I ask you a question? Has the statement of this witness been uploaded in e-court? Because I'm trying to find it, and I can't find it. Maybe it's my lack of technological awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'll try to assist you, Your Honour. The ID number is 2D05 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 2D05-0272 in B/C/S, and in English, it's 2D04-0109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DER WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I can't find it in the tendered documents nor in the Defence release documents, but maybe I need some assistance from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I kindly ask for admission of this certificate, of course, to keep reserve for additional translation for the -- from the official service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask two things. One, I would ask that it be marked for identification until we have the correct translation. I don't think it'd be wise to admit something that we now know is an erroneous translation. And secondly, I would ask Mr. Cepic -- we admitted a similar document yesterday. I would ask that that document be reviewed, and if it, too, has an error in its translation, I would ask that Mr. Cepic bring that to our attention so that the Chamber may deal with that properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the hospital record?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Another certificate from the same priest was introduced with, I believe, the first witness, Mr. Zivkovic, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Okay. We'll mark it for identification, pending translation from the services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DER WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Excuse me to interrupt again, but I have now retrieved the document that you referred to in e-court and it's another document, so this is not the statement of this witness, document 2D05-0272. I was trying to follow. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologize, Your Honour. This is a version in B/C/S. Maybe I made confusion. In English is 2D04-0109. Witness statement, and it is on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The registrar's going to print the document for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologize, I'm not so skillful with these electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DER WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Neither am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to do my best. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Popadic [as interpreted]. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Bugarski, I'm to your right. I'm Dermot Groome, and I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. The first question I'd like to ask you is, you've told us that by profession you're a salesman. What do you sell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I'm a salesman. I have cattle feed in my store, concentrates for cattle feed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where do you currently live?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: In Krtinska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you live in the same home that you lived in in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have a phone in the house?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have a phone in the house in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've lived all of your life in Krtinska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to be a man who enjoys good health?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I have blood pressure a bit on the high side, but that's because of my advanced age.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But aside from the high blood pressure that many of us get as we age, you have no other ailments that you suffer from. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to discuss with you your relationship to Sredoje Lukic. Am I correct in saying that you know him for over 25 years?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's 25 years, but I've known him since 1983 or 1984. I can't be more precise. When he got married. I've known him ever since he got married.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And throughout that period of 24, 25 years, you've always enjoyed good relationships with him and his family. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. From that point onwards, because I had known his wife from before. She is the sister of my brother-in-law's wife. My wife's brother's sister-in-law is his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand that. Have you celebrated holidays with Sredoje Lukic's family?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, mostly at Milojko Popadic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when's the last time you celebrated a holiday with Sredoje Lukic and his family?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: And can't say precisely. It was usually around St. George's Day because my brother-in-law celebrates that holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that St. George's Day this past year -- or I'm sorry, did you celebrate St. George's Day --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No, no. Well, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever celebrate Vidovdan with him or St. Vitus's Day?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, in my village we do not celebrate St. Vitus's Day. It's just a holiday that we acknowledge, but we do not celebrate it specially in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say that it's not celebrated in your village, are you saying that it's the custom that no one in the village would celebrate Vidovdan Day?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: In my village, nobody celebrates Vidovdan. We just don't work on that day. It is a major holiday of ours, and nobody works on that day. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think that we have a problem in transcript. It is quite --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- it is quite different from B/C/S in English. Second sentence on 25th page, line 1, in my village nobody celebrates Vidovdan. We just don't work on that day. Witness said [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: According to Mr. Cepic, what is that supposed to mean, unless it means "nobody works."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is different meaning than nobody works, but is the issue -- maybe better -- it would be better translation, "acknowledge of that holiday," or something like commemorate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic is inaudible. Could he kindly speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you're being asked to speak into the microphone. What do you say is the correct translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness did not say "nobody works on that day." He said something like -- I'll try to be interpreter. Acknowledge that holiday or -- I need assistance from Mr. -- commemorate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That nobody commemorates that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No one commemorate that day but they acknowledge that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not commemorated but it's acknowledged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a suggestion. It's quite difficult to conduct an examination and have lengthy discourses about possible different interpretations. There's actually a procedure for doing this. There's a sheet of paper which Mr. Cepic can take. He can simply mark the line that he has issue with, mark what he thinks is the error, and then that will be reviewed by the interpreters and the transcript recorders during the course of the day, and it seems to me that we should be bound by the professionals that are sitting in the booth and not be entering into a discourse in the middle of my examination about what a particular word might mean. I'd ask that we follow the procedure designated for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Mr. Cepic. There is a procedure to be followed, so unless it is something that is particularly urgent and of great significance to the understanding of the evidence, please follow that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and just one sentence with your leave. Just to avoid any misleading later for cross-examination of Mr. Groome. That is the point why I raise that issue. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to take you to your statement which is now in evidence. In paragraph 8 of your statement, you say: "Sredoje Lukic would occasionally go to Visegrad, and he would usually call me when he was coming or going." Do you recall saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Could you please expound on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me call it up in front of you so you can actually see the statement that you signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we see paragraph 8 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that's being called up, I believe it refers to the period of time in the spring, summer, of 1992 that you were referring, but we're calling it up now, and you should see it on your screen in front of you in the next few seconds. While it's being called up, let me ask you a couple of other questions. During -- you also say in your statement that during this period, spring, summer of 1992, Sredoje Lukic was looking for work in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: That's correct. It is correct that he was trying to get employment in Belgrade. When I let him the apartment and he entered my parents' home and after he stabilized after the problems he'd had, as far as I know he would go to Belgrade because he was -- he told me he was trying to get employment using the services of a relative that he had over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we heard about some of that yesterday. Could you ask you to please, if possible, answer my question yes or no or as briefly as you can. We are -- we do have to be mindful of the time here. Was it your understanding that he was unemployed at this time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, that was my understanding because he had come from Visegrad with the intention of not going back there, and his plans were to try to find a job in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know if during this period his wife Vidjenka was working?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No, she was not employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, now paragraph 8 is up on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we move down a little bit so the witness can see paragraph 7 as well. Oh, it's on another page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, let us know if you want to look at paragraph 7, but let's see if that doesn't remind you of the context in which you said that: "Sredoje Lukic would occasionally go to Visegrad and he would usually call me when he was going or coming" -- or "coming or going." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question for you, sir, is if he was out of work, if he was looking for work in Belgrade, what was your understanding about why he was returning, coming and going from Visegrad during this period?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Can I now? Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know? If you know.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, what you asked me about happened afterwards when he could not find employment in Belgrade. When he'd realized that he could not find a job in Belgrade, it was then that he returned to Visegrad. He was looking for work in Belgrade around the start of May in 1992. He was traveling to Belgrade, and when he realized that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, when he was going and coming from Visegrad, what was it -- what was your understanding about why he was going and coming from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, to work, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you're aware of the incident in which Sredoje Lukic and Niko Vujicic were held captive and tortured by Muslims in Visegrad. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I saw it on RTS television in April. It was an afternoon when I saw Sredoje and some other people on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you were aware of it. So my question to you is, is can you describe what Sredoje Lukic was like after that incident? Did you notice a noticeable change in him as a result of that incident?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Are you asking me about that footage or did I see it on TV footage?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, not about the footage itself. I'm asking you about when you met or saw Sredoje Lukic after that incident, after he was released, did you notice any differences in him, in his personality, in his behavior, after having undergone that torture and being burnt by these Muslim captives?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I noticed when he came to visit his family a day or two after that TV broadcast, my wife had gone to visit her brother, and I saw that he was despondent, in a bad mood, even afraid, and he even showed me certain scars on his arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what -- you've made some motion to both of your wrists. What were the scars that you observed on his body?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I saw redness of skin. I asked him what was this all about. He said, I was tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see where he had been burned?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I saw when he raised his shirt that he had visible injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could you describe those injuries for us?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, there were bruises, and there was redness, the same as I had seen on the TV footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he express any anger at what -- about his treatment?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember if he was angry, but he was despondent, very silent. I could see that something was going on. I mean, I didn't spend a long time with him, perhaps an hour before I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct in saying that you are the brother-in-law of the next witness, Milojko Popadic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: He's my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is making distinction between terms of relation that do not exist in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So to be clear, you are married to his sister, Milojka?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You didn't provide that information in your statement. The statement that we have before you, you don't inform us that you have that relationship to Mr. Popadic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, nobody asked me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe your relationship with Veroljub Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, Veroljub Zivkovic lives in the same village as I do. Not in the same hamlet, though. He lives on a farm, an agricultural property called Mladost. We've known each other --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I interrupted you. I was going to ask you, how long have you known Mr. Zivkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, forever, since he was born. It's the same village, only a different hamlet. He was born on the Mladost property. I was born in Krtinska hamlet. That's how we know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you always enjoyed a good relationship with him and his family?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Depends on how you understand it. We are on good business terms. He's a good locksmith and autobody repairman, and Milojko Popadic, as you know, a haulier. He has many trucks and whenever something would break down, he would give it to Veroljub to repair. I brought two trucks to my own son when he turned 18, and Veroljub set these trucks right, put them in good shape. Now he's working somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just so you understand how it works here, it takes a few seconds before I actually hear what you say, so the long pause is not me waiting for you to answer more. It's simply me waiting to hear, so again, if I could ask you to please try to keep your answers brief and allow me to ask follow-up questions. Thank you, sir. I want to now ask you about where Sredoje Lukic lived in Obrenovac when he moved his family. Can you tell us where he lived when he first came to Obrenovac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, in the month of March, he brought his family, that's to say his wife and children, and his brother. I saw him then when he arrived in the end March, bringing his wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And he first lived in the house of Mr. Popadic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Popadic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Subsequently, he moved to an apartment that you owned that used to be your parents' home or apartment, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's your best memory as to when he moved from the Popadic house to the apartment that you owned?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he paying you rent?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in thinking that at that time there were a number of Serb families living in Eastern Bosnia that were moving to the Belgrade area and it would have been possible for you to have allowed a -- it would have been possible for you to have rented out that apartment for some money? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time it was the beginning of the war, and the circumstances were straight. It's not really well seen in our parts to make a profit on somebody who is in a bad situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did he remain in your apartment altogether?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: From the end of April, he stayed perhaps until the end of October, I'd say, if I'm not mistaken. I know that his daughter Bojana started the second year of school while living our village, and then after that they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So he stayed in your apartment until October 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you just said, and I see it in your statement, that Sredoje's brother also moved to Obrenovac. Which brother was that? What was the name of that brother?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Not that I know of. I don't know that his brother moved to Obrenovac. Instead --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me read what you have -- what you have in paragraph 3 of the statement which is in evidence. It says: "In March 1992, Sredoje Lukic's family came to Obrenovac, as did his brother's family." Do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: That's true, but they only came together for an hour or two. I don't know if they spent the night at Milojko Popadic's house. All I know is that when I went to visit, they were no longer there. Only Sredoje's family was there. They could have moved on to Belgrade, perhaps. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, that clears that. I wanted to talk to you now about the feast of the Holy Trinity. What day -- the Holy Trinity occurs on a different date each year. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Not really. The Holy Trinity's always on a Sunday, always on a Sunday. Only the dates are different, 50 days from Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So some years it might be the 12th of June, the 16th of June. It could even be in May depending upon if Easter comes early in a particular year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure about May, but perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What day was the feast of the Holy Trinity on in the year 2000? Do you know what date, what date in June?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Which day?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know the date, the numerical date?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No, no. I would have to look up a calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell me what date it fell on in 1995, or am I correct in assuming that you'd have difficulty doing that as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No, I can't do that. You can see it in the church calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, who told you that in 1992 the feast of the Holy Trinity fell on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This question is misleading because this witness never mentioned 14th of June in his statement. He just mentioned Holy Trinity celebration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that from, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may have a minute to check the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, is it your evidence that you do not know the date of the Holy Trinity in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, now I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my question to you is, now that you know, who told you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did he find out?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you find out?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I found out from a calendar provided by - I don't know who it was provided by, and you can look it up at my parents' calendar - they keep all this stuff. And I saw it here. It's somewhere -- lawyer Cepic has it, and he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it was Mr. Cepic that informed you that the feast of the Holy Trinity fell on the 14th of June in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is misleading of witness. Witness clearly stated in his statement, he never mentioned 14th of June, and now Mr. Groome putting his word to him. The statement is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the lawyer [sic] has just said: "Lawyer Cepic has it, and he told me that." I'm simply confirming what the witness has said. I'm not confined to what has been placed in this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's quite so. The question is based on the answer provided by the witness, Mr. Cepic, so it's not objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, but in a moment of -- in a moment of when he gave the statement, he didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. It's not in the statement. I don't see it in the statement, 14th of June, but the evidence that has been led in cross-examination provides a foundation for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he said that on preparation he saw the church calendar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but he just told Mr. Cepic [sic] that a lawyer told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that is why Mr. Groome is asking the question. It's based on his answer, the witness's answer. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, when did Mr. Cepic tell you that it was the 14th of June? Was it the first time you met him or some subsequent time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, what date was it -- practically yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Practically yesterday. So yesterday, Mr. Cepic told you that it was --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I saw it, also, on this calendar, a photocopy of the calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which calendar are you referring to? Who showed you a calendar?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: There's a copy here, I don't know if you can show it on the screen, a copy of an Orthodox church calendar for the month of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe we have seen that. It's in evidence. So my question to you is, who showed you that calendar?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cepic showed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, now, I want to talk to you about celebrations in the Serb Orthodox church in general. Would I be correct in saying that Serbs are a people who enjoy their friends, their families, and enjoy many celebrations throughout the year?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I need for the record to record --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And there are some holidays that everyone who is Serb Orthodox celebrates, there are holidays that families celebrate, and there are holidays that villages celebrate, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you be able to estimate approximately how many different celebrations you, your family, would celebrate over the course of a year?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: My family, my household has one family patron saint's day. That's St. Stephen of Decani, and we have the celebration of the Holy Trinity with the whole village, and we take several non-working days in a year. There is a difference between a celebration and a day off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, my question to you is, is the -- we have your statement about what happened in 1992. Why are you so sure that it happened on the feast of the Holy Trinity and not one of the other many celebrations or feasts that are celebrated by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, if you could clarify a little what happened. If you could be more precise. I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, we have your statement which records how Sredoje Lukic and Mr. Popadic came to your house one evening after an argument at the store. My question to you is, why are you so sure 15 years later that it was the feast of the Holy Trinity and not one of the other feasts that are celebrated by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I can remember that year because in my household, in my broader family, some difficult things happened. I was in mourning for my dead brother, my brother who had died the previous year in November; and in March 1992, the son of my wife's brother died. He had been wounded, and he could not be transported to Sarajevo and on to Uzice and he died from his wounds, so both my wife and I were in mourning. This incident had happened in Sokolac. It was Zjelko Popadic who died. So, that year was really hard for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just let me ask you a quick question about this nephew who died. Was he killed during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: He is the nephew of my wife. He is the son of her brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I understand. Now, was he killed in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Not in the conflict. If you want to be precise, he was a receptionist in a hotel, and what exactly happened, I don't know. All we know is that he was wounded, and he was driven away towards Sarajevo. There was some roadblocks. He was turned back towards Uzice. They ran into another roadblock. He died, and he was buried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that a natural death, or was he killed by someone?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I know he was wounded, but how exactly that happened, whether it was some sort of clash or a conflict, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know if the people that wounded him were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. Some people said that it was a self-inflicted wound. Other people said he was wounded in a skirmish. There were contradicting stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the roadblocks that prevented him from getting to Sarajevo for treatment, were they roadblocks that were set up by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: You know, I really can't tell you now. I don't know if they were Muslims or the other ones. What I don't know, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if you don't know, just please, let me know, and I'll ask you another question. Now, the argument that occurred between Sredoje Lukic and the shopkeeper on what you say is Holy Trinity Day, I want to be clear. You were not present in the grocery store when there was this argument over a deposit for some beer bottles, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zivkovic, the only witness to personally witness it, does not characterize it as a very serious dispute. Am I correct that your only connection with this incident is that sometime later in the evening Sredoje Lukic and Milojko Popadic came to your home and mentioned it to you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who told you? Sredoje or Milojko?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Milojko told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Milojko say that he was present during the dispute?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: He didn't tell me he had been present. Do you want a longer explanation, or do you want a yes or no answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A yes or no will suffice. How long did it take them to tell you what happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, we stayed together for about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that the only thing that you spoke about during that ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We talked only about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It seems that the whole exchange only took a few minutes, the dispute over the bottles, so are you saying that it took ten minutes for them to tell you about this dispute over the beer bottles?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: They were not telling me about beer bottles. If you want me to be precise, outside my yard a red Aleko vehicle stopped, and it was driven by Milojko Popadic. I was sitting outside on the terrace with my guests, and I looked outside, and it seemed strange to me that Milojko Popadic was driving Sredoje's car. So they stopped outside my gate. Milojko, Sredoje, and Sredoje's -- and Milojko's son came out. They greet my children, and I motioned with my hand for Milojko to come up. It's strange to me that he's not coming out. I -- and he shows me with his hand I'm not coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, what time did they arrive at your house?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: It's hard to say what time it was. It was summer time. The first dusk. It was already getting dark. I can't tell you how -- I can't tell you the hour, but it was already getting dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you offer them a drink?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I didn't have time because he wouldn't come out of the car, although I was motioning him to get out, and he was saying, Let go, I don't want to drink, I have problems. I asked, With whom? And he said, With Sredoje up there at Mladost. He went into a shop to get some drink, and it turns out he had a quarrel with a shopkeeper about some packaging. He wouldn't give him the beer without the packaging, and so he wouldn't come out. He was supposed to drive Sredoje to the house where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have that in your statement. Sredoje did get out of the car, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it appear that he had been drinking?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, he was a bit -- not much, but as he was coming out, my son grabbed him by the upper arm. Sredoje was always a cheerful man. I wouldn't say he was drunk, but he was -- he had had a few drinks, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Milojko Popadic, he the same, he had had a few drinks?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No, no. He was only angry, but I wouldn't say he had been drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how about yourself? Did you have any drink to celebrate Holy Trinity feast?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: That year, I didn't really feel like drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, is it your testimony that this brief conversation of about ten minutes about this dispute over a deposit for a crate of beer bottles left such an impression upon you that you have a clear and vivid memory of it 16 years later?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, you know, what struck me was that somebody came up to my door and didn't come in and didn't want to join us for that celebration. We spent more time arguing about why he wouldn't come out than about the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So what's more memorable to you is not what they said about the dispute at the store but the fact that you offered them a drink and they did not come into your house, they just kept going. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. They were standing there, but they didn't really come into the house, and I remember the reason why they didn't come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I must put it to you plainly. I submit that something like offering hospitality to guests who arrive at our homes and it's politely refused is a rather common occurrence, and I submit to you that it's implausible that you could have such a vivid memory of this event 16 years after the fact.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I remember it because there are several things there during that holiday that moved me, and I remember that year. That year for us was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, what was the weather that evening?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's silly to talk about it. I didn't think about that. June is always shifty. Holy Trinity is in June. In June, there's usually a development of clouds in the afternoons --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, it seems that you don't have a vivid or clear memory about the weather that day, and what you're advising me now is how the weather in June is generally, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: As I said, the weather was changing. There was some clouds. There was probably some rain, light rain, but I really cannot remember, but I do believe that there was some cloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, do you know a name [sic] by a name of Dragoljub Stakic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: From my village or my parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Also known as Lalika, if that's him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where does he live?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: He lives currently in Obrenovac, but he has a house in Krtinska. His mother's house is there, and he has a brother there. His street is adjacent to my street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, unless you're going to finish shortly, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the court officer has asked for just a moment to take care of some administrative things.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Your Honour, just to have it reflected in the transcript, the Defence certificate is admitted as 2D48, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, we were talking about a person by the name of Dragoljub Stakic. My question for you is, did he live in Krtinska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see him this night?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did you last see him?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: You mean in recent days?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I saw him driving some machinery into the base. That's that last thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long ago was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Some five or six days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, just returning for a second to Serb holidays, another Serb holiday that's celebrated very close to Holy Trinity is the feast of St. George, which is celebrated on the 6th of May every year. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony, you were describing this relative Zjelko Popadic who died prior to this feast of the Holy Trinity. What relationship is Zjelko Popadic to Milojko Popadic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: You mean as a cousin or relative?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. What is the relationship between the two?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: That is a nephew, his cousin's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So Zjelko Popadic is Milojko Popadic's nephew?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, earlier today at transcript page 40, lines 7 to 8, you said: "I was sitting outside on the terrace" of your house with guests. Can I ask you to list for us, who were the guests that were sitting on your terrace that evening when Sredoje Lukic and Milojko Popadic arrived? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, since it was already dusk, the kums had left. Who remained was my sister with her family, waiting for the bus for Obrenovac.
