utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what's your sister's name?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Liposava Kuturovic [phoen] and Kuturovic Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And any other guests there at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: And her husband Kuturovic Zivota, but unfortunately he is no longer with us. These were the inner circle of guests. Whoever had a car had already left, and they were still waiting for the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you in part remember which Holy Trinity this was because of its relationship to the start of the war. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, we need to have an audible answer that we can record on the transcript, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the people of the former Yugoslavia have had the misfortune of suffering through several wars, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps the closest the people of Krtinska came to feeling the effects of war was when a NATO bomb landed right in the village of Krtinska on the 28th of March of 1999. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: 28th? Well, could you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I won't -- let's ignore the date for a minute. Do you remember a NATO bomb landing unexploded in the village of Krtinska, it was meant for the power plant nearby, but do you remember a bomb actually landing in the village in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No, no. This was later. That was 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm talking about, in 1999. Do you recall an incident where a NATO bomb landed in the village of Krtinska?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. It was power transmission, a line. One NATO bomb fell there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you also recall not too far from Krtinska, a US Stealth Bomber actually crashed on the territory of Serbia? Do you recall that, around the same time period?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Near -- close to Sabac, across the Sava River. Yes, I do remember. There was a village there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's your best memory as to the date when the bomb fell in Krtinska?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, it didn't fall on Krtinska. It fell in a line -- in a field close to a power transmission line. As for the date, it's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you have any reason to think I'd be incorrect if I said that it occurred on the 28th of March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: It wasn't March. It only could have been -- well, I know I was in the field planting paprikas. It only could have been in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could it have been another year other than 1999? Might I be wrong about that as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, this happened during NATO's bombardment. You're not wrong. I know that I was out in the field planting paprikas, together with my wife, when this happened -- well, it was May, the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if this verbal dispute did in fact occur on the first celebration of Holy Trinity after the war, isn't this the war that you really mean, the war that really had an effect on the village of Krtinska, the bombardment in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: This is not very clear to me. What did you mean by that, whether we were in jeopardy? Could you please expound and explain this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I have some sympathy with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question wasn't very clear to me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you say that one of the ways you fix which Holy Trinity feast day was its relationship to the war, and my suggestion to you is that the war that you really remember is the war where a bomb fell not far from your village in 1999, that the Holy Trinity that you're referring to is really the first Holy Trinity after the NATO bombardment of your village. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I know what you mean and what you want to ask me. Well, the beginning of something is the most tragic thing, and then people grow used to their circumstances, and we did. Together with the start of the war, I -- my wife lost her brother's son, I had lost my brother, so these stick out in my memory. I do remember those events that you refer to, but we'd grown accustomed to such events. I'm not sure whether I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You have. Now, in addition to providing Mr. Sredoje Lukic with an alibi for the 14th of June, you also provide one for later in the month on the 27th of June. In your statement in paragraph 9, you state that two weeks after the Holy Trinity celebration, the day before Vidovdan celebration, Sredoje Lukic and Niko Vujicic stopped by your home. Is that correct? Yes or no if you can.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: You know how it is. They didn't come on Vidovdan itself. I had been in contact with Sredoje Lukic before St. Vitus's Day over the phone a couple of days prior to that. Prior to that, I used to slaughter pigs for him and after that, as well, and this was what we had discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, a lot of those details are in the statement, so I just have very specific questions, and my question to you is, is that the day before Vidovdan Day, it's your evidence that Sredoje Lukic and Niko Vujicic came to your home, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't come to my home. We were in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the record records you as saying that you spoke with Sredoje over the phone. I thought you had testified earlier that you did not have a phone in 1992. Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It wasn't a frequent occurrence for people to have phones in the village. There were no mobile phones. There were maybe one or two or three people in the village who had phones. But in my company, the oil plant, I had a phone. The phone number was at the time 8721567, and this is the only telephone that I used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was Sredoje Lukic when he was calling you or you called him? Where was he located at the time you had this conversation by phone?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I think that he was in Visegrad. I don't know, but I think that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when did you have this telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Some two or three days, so if this -- the dates he was supposed to fetch the meat was 27th, then it was on the 23rd or 24th that we had spoken. He had asked me whether I could prepare one suckling pig for the freezer, and he said that he would take it to bring home to Visegrad when he would next be coming to Belgrade and this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it's your evidence that on the 23rd or 24th, Sredoje Lukic called you from Visegrad and asked you to prepare a suckling pig for the Vidovdan feast, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was meant for St. Vitus's day, but the purpose was for him to take it with him over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So he was going to come, collect this suckling pig, and bring it back to Visegrad and cook it and eat it in Visegrad? That was your understanding?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What time did Sredoje Lukic and Niko Vujicic arrive?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, towards the evening in the afternoon, in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is your best estimate about the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: It was summer time, late afternoon, 6, 7, maybe 6. I cannot be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just clarifying something you just said, you said at 49, line 7, that Sredoje Lukic -- I'll quote what the record says: "He said that he would take it to bring home to Visegrad when he would next be coming to Belgrade and this area." Do I take from that that it was your understanding that Sredoje Lukic considered Visegrad still his home? Did he use those words, I'm bringing it home to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Who else was home at the time that he came for the pig which you had prepared?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: At my home?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: My wife and me. Wife and the children, but my wife and I prepared the meat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you also say in your statement which is in evidence that Niko Vujicic also had his family in Obrenovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I do know that they were there. I'm not close to that person, Niko. I knew him through Sredoje. Maybe I saw him once or twice very briefly. On that occasion, he was sitting in the car. They did not go out of the car, and I had heard that he had family in a different street in Obrenovac, in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that Sredoje Lukic and Niko Vujicic had a close relationship?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Most probably. They were driving around together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know that Niko Vujicic was also a police officer in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I heard about that. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also know that Niko Vujicic was also held captive at the same time Sredoje Lukic was?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, now, the Chamber is in possession of a report alleging that both Sredoje Lukic and Niko Vujicic formed a paramilitary group after they were released from captivity. My question to you is, other than being held captive by Muslims and being tortured and everything, mistreatment, is there anything else that you're aware of that occurred to both of those men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll just let him answer, and then you can ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was a long question. Happened to them or what they did? Your question was rather long, too long for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question to you is, are you aware of anything else that happened to Niko Vujicic and Sredoje Lukic together, something similar to being held captive in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I know that they were policemen, but after that, I don't know. I can't say. There's some 200 kilometers between our two respective cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your evidence is you're not aware of any other event other than them being held captive that occurred to both Vujicic and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe later. What I heard was that Niko was wounded, but I can't tell you when. I can't specify the year. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, just a minute. Mr. Cepic had had a point. I don't know whether he still wants to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I think the witness clarified that -- I could object. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, again on page 51 at line 18 -- I'll read you your answer. It's beginning on line 17: "I know that they were policemen, but after that, I don't know. I can't say. There's some 200 kilometers between our two respective cities." Again, this seems to suggest that you see Sredoje Lukic as not living in Krtinska but living in Visegrad. Am I correct in concluding that from what you've said here?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, he was for a long period at home after he'd been held captive and came home, thinking that he would not be returning. I can explain that. In that time, he used to go to Belgrade frequently. His plans were to find employment there, but as I understood it, since he could not find a job in Belgrade, he returned most probably to his job in Visegrad. I don't know whether that's correct. Later on, we would see each other over weekends when he would come. I don't know when he had the time to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So back to the preparation of the meat for Sredoje Lukic, you state that the purpose of Sredoje Lukic stopping by was to tell you that he would be unable to take some meat that you had in your freezer and he had arranged to carry to Visegrad, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 9 of your statement that's now in evidence: "We had agreed earlier that I would prepare food for them, pork, to be precise, so they could put it in a freezer and bring it to their family in Visegrad." Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, if Niko Vujicic has his family in Obrenovac, if Sredoje Lukic has his family in Krtinska, who is the family they are bringing what sounds to be quite a substantial amount of meat to in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I think that Sredoje Lukic had a brother, father, mother over there. Family also includes parents, not just the wife and the kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, a suckling pig, am I right in thinking that it's something that can fit into a car? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, it was 120 kilograms reduced to 70, 80 when it was cut up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it is something that would fit on either the backseat of a car or in the trunk of a car. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I couldn't really say. They did not stop for long, and this was the point of the whole thing. I was miffed. They came and explained, Brane, sorry, have you to make do with this meat because we cannot transport it. Now, I have some obligations. I have some people, passengers to drive. Sorry, he said. And then I was upset, thinking, What am I going to do with all that meat? And he put me in a fait accompli situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A suckling pig, how old is the pig? How many months before a pig is no longer considered a suckling pig?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: 120 kilos, that is a 7- or 8-month up to one-year-old pig, 120 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would fit into the trunk of a car; am I not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, he can fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It can fit into the trunk of a car. Is that correct? Again, we need --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've said that Sredoje Lukic said he could not take the suckling pig back to Visegrad because he had some passengers in his car, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Supposed to take that over, but I did not see at the time whether there were or not, or he was supposed to pick somebody up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe you say in your statement that he took -- there were two acquaintances that were supposed to also go back to Visegrad with him, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, he said that he was supposed to pick some people up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and he told you that he was leaving for Visegrad early the next morning on Vidovdan Day, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, whether he left immediately or on the next morning, I cannot really say. They just started the engine and left. Whether they went to this apartment in the street adjacent to mine, I don't know. I cannot tell you -- [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The interpretation stopped. Let me just wait a moment to see. Is there a difficulty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the interpreter whether he or she wishes to have the witness conclude the sentence so we can get the end of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, would you please just repeat the end of what you are saying. Yes, you, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying -- I was saying I was in an awkward position, not knowing what to do with the meat that he was supposed to collect. I didn't know where they were going. He was supposed to pay me for the meat and collect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he ever actually then come back and pick up this meat?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did he do that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: The next weekend he came, I cannot remember exactly now, but I know the meat was placed in the freezer. We crammed it in there somehow, and the next time he came to visit his family, he collected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, then my question to you is, if the meat wasn't for Vidovdan, and you're not sure when it was that he came back to collect the meat, how are you so sure that he first came to tell you he could not take the meat the day before Vidovdan? Why are you so sure about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't come the next day after St. Vitus Day because I wouldn't be working. I wouldn't be open on St. Vitus Day. Nobody works. It's a big holiday. That's how I remember. I remember it also because he created problems for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you see his wife or children either this day or the next day, Vidovdan Day?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: The next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You did see his wife. Where did you see his wife?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Around where she lives, my second house. My wife or I would regularly go there once or twice a day because we had some animals there, a small farm that I kept up. I sold animals to complement my salary. The salaries were very low at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when he came to your house to tell you that he was not taking the meat, did he mention to you where he was earlier in the day?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything then, not where he had been or where he was going, but when we talked on the phone, he told me he was supposed to come to Belgrade, to come our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How was he dressed when he came?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: You mean in civilian clothes or in -- he was in civilian clothes. Summer clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, we made a request of your government for your criminal record, and we were provided with the information about two prior convictions that you have. They are some years ago, so I don't want to spend too much time on them, but I do want to ask you a question about -- a very brief question about them. The first is an offense entitled, "Serious criminal offenses against public safety causing the death of one or more persons and damaging of safety equipment at working sites out of negligence," in violation of Article 194, paragraph 4, and Article 189, paragraph 3, of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia. Your conviction was on the 4th of April, 1984. Am I correct in concluding from the title of the conviction that a person died as a result of your conduct? Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: It is difficult to talk about, but it was not a fatality that was involved. I was responsible just as manager in that factory. The man stepped on a conveyor belt that was not properly installed. The maintenance service did not install it properly, and it ripped his leg off. I was given a two-year suspended sentence. That man is not dead. He's still alive. He works as a receptionist in my company. That's the real truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I accept that. Sir, you -- the record also says that you served a sentence of five months' imprisonment and then were placed on two years of parole. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Correct. I said suspended sentence. I did not serve the sentence, but if something had happened on top of it, then I would have. I was really convicted, although I had nothing to do with the incident, but still I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, do you have something?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I have a feeling that my learned friend Mr. Groome doesn't know the system of sanctions in my country. Witness already clarified that. But witness already clarified that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't you educate him privately?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'll try that. I'll try that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're coming to an end now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not too -- just one and a half more pages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One and a half more pages. Now, I neglected to say at the outset that in the last session, if there is one, my two colleagues will be sitting under 15 bis to allow me to carry out other duties. And in fact, I was hoping to finish at 12 to give myself some time for preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I certainly will be finished with this witness before that time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the second conviction is from the 18th of November, 1993, during the war, and the conviction was for a violation of Article 161, paragraph 2, entitled, "Forest theft with the aim of selling the timber cut." In this case, the information we were provided indicated that you were sentenced to three months with a two-year period of parole. Is it correct that this conviction arises from illegal logging activities that you were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: There is some truth in that. I cut my own trees, which were not registered. Those were my trees. When the ranger came, he seized the timber and I was punished because I had not registered it. It was my wood up to the Sava River, and I was punished because I had not registered it. It was safe to log, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'm finished with that line of inquiry. And I want to ask you, your first meeting with Mr. Cepic was arranged by Mr. Popadic. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he arranged it. I saw Cepic in that yard, the yard of my parents where Sredoje used to live. Now I'm building a small workshop there. Popadic was coming up, and there was a man with him. That man said, I am the Defence counsel of Sredoje Lukic, could I talk to you please, and that's how we met. And in the conversation, it came up that he asked me, Did Sredoje used to live here? I said yes, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that was in the summer of 2007, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Yes. August, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And they met you in front of your home?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: In the yard of the house where Sredoje used to live, my second house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, once Mr. Popadic introduced Mr. Cepic to you, he didn't leave. He remained there when you spoke with Mr. Cepic. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly. I think Popadic went to see my son and the workers who were busy a bit further down setting up some nets and I don't know what. I think Cepic and I were talking on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The statement that is now in evidence is dated the 5th of January, 2008. Do you remember giving it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: This year, yes. Yes, the 5th, between Christmas and New Year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The other witness statements are dated in November 2007. Was there a reason that you were unavailable to, well, give a statement until January 2008?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How could this witness know where other witnesses gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm asking him whether he was unavailable.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... base for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that was asked was, was there a reason that you were unavailable to give a statement in January 2008. Is that the question you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The question is, Your Honour, whether he was unavailable prior to January of 2008 to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, so what's the problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Groome also quoted that other witnesses gave the statements in November, why you did not give the statement in November? This is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but the question is, was there a reason why you were unavailable to give a statement until January 2008. Can you answer that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. I have huge obligations, the farming, the work, the shop, caring for my child, health concerns, et cetera. When you put all that together, he - that's true - called and tried several times to make an appointment, but I couldn't make it, and then on the 5th of January, I went to see him. He did -- he had called me in November or December, I don't know, asking me to come over, and I couldn't make it then. But when the season, the working season had already passed, that's when I could make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you -- who was present when you gave your statement in January 2008?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: The lawyer, Mr. Cepic, in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on the 5th of June, 2008, my investigator had made an appointment to interview you. Do you remember that appointment being made?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And after they interviewed the person just before you, I believe it was Mr. Popadic, we were informed that you would not be coming to the interview. Why did you not come to the interview that had been arranged?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago I tried to explain that I have a great workload. It was the season where I had a lot of work, and I was not in the greatest of health at that time. The doctor had sent me to make an EKG, and I took a long time, and when I came back home, my children told me that somebody had asked for me on the phone. I thought they would call back the next day or the day after, but they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is the reason that you did not come for that scheduled interview because you had too much work or because you were ill?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I was a bit ill, and perhaps it's my fault I didn't understand it that seriously. I thought, Who would ever want me, Branko Bugarski, to come to The Hague? I don't know if you understand me. I did not really understand the matter. It's entirely my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. We were told that you were experiencing a heart problem along with high blood pressure and that you would be unavailable for a period of days to be interviewed. That's what we were told. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Most probably, yes, and even now if you took my blood pressure, it would be 120, 115 at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, at the beginning of my examination of you I asked you about your health, and you said aside from the high blood pressure, you were in good health. So was this the first time you had a problem with your heart, the day of this interview?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: No. I hadn't properly understood you. I thought you meant whether I'm feeling fine now. Maybe I misunderstood, but there are enough documents as far as that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the last line of questioning that I have for you has to do with the media coverage that surrounded this case, and what I want to explore with you is, why -- if you knew this information and you were good friends with Sredoje Lukic, why did it take so long for you to come forward with information that could have helped exonerate an innocent man?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, I do feel guilty about that. I hadn't really understood it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you were aware of the many media articles and television shows that covered not only this case because the Vasiljevic case which deals with some similar events. You were aware of the media coverage and that Sredoje Lukic was accused of some very serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, the media are the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you were aware from the media that Sredoje Lukic was charged with crimes, that he had been arrested, that there was some consideration of sending the case to Bosnia. You were aware of all of that from the media, were you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I hadn't understood that it was really the way it was and that I can be of any help. But later, I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who was the first person to make you understand that what you had information about could help Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, as Cepic came and made inquiries, from that time on I started thinking that it's a serious matter -- I mean, at first I -- that's the first time I understood it, really. Until then, I was too involved in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many times did you speak with Mr. Popadic about this case?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: With Popadic about this case? He is a haulier. He often travels chasing income. I am trying to make ends meet in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, my question is very specific. How many times have you spoken to Mr. Popadic about this case?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Well, from time to time when we were in contact sometimes, I can't tell you now how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once a week? Once a month?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps we saw each other once a month. My wife went to see them more often. In winter, possibly we could see each other more often than in the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you discuss with him your account of these events from June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: Maybe -- I don't know. Maybe we talked. I asked him if he remembered that Sredoje had come. I mean, it was recently, and he said -- I don't know. Who can remember all these things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you must be bringing the cross-examination to an end now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just a couple of more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you asked him if he remembered that Sredoje had come, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: He wasn't able to tell me. He couldn't answer me because he wasn't at home. He's always on the road; he's a haulier. And why would I have to ask him when I know myself that it was on the eve of a great holiday, Vidovdan, St. Vitus Day? It's a big deal for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you travel here to The Hague with Mr. Popadic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR BUGARSKI
utterances.text: By plane, yes. We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Maybe just a few questions, Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just before you ask the questions. Witness, I'm not sure whether you understood the line of questioning from the Prosecutor, but let me make it plain to you that what the Prosecutor is saying is that your whole evidence is nothing but a tissue of lies and that you are lying because Sredoje Lukic is your friend. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can I answer to that? It's not true that it's a tissue of lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you come here to lie to protect your friend? Because remember, you took an oath. You made a declaration to speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth. In a few days, I'll turn 60. I would not have come here to tell lies. I know this man as a good man, a sociable man, always ready to share a good joke. I never knew him as a criminal. It's only for that reason that I made this long journey. I have many things to do in my life. I don't want to lie. I have my family. I have children. I have grandchildren. That's a hard thing to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. Let me just explain that I'm not saying that you're lying. I haven't reached the stage in the proceedings where I have to make a decision on that. I'm explaining to you what the Prosecutor was trying to say. I'm putting it to you very bluntly and squarely that what he was saying is that the whole thing, your whole evidence is nothing but a concoction, a fabrication, and you have said, No, it is not. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what to say. You told me that I'm lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't tell you that you are lying. What I told you is that the effect of the cross-examination is a suggestion that you're lying. I am not yet at the stage of the proceedings where I have to make a decision as to whether you're a witness of truth or whether you're telling lies. But what the cross-examiner, what the Prosecutor was in effect saying to you, although he didn't put it as bluntly as I have, is that your whole evidence is fabricated in order to protect your friend, and you have said no. So we'll leave it at that, and I thank you on behalf of the Chamber for coming to the Tribunal. You have come from far. I thank you for coming to give evidence. It is now over, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just say one thing? It's the first time in my life that somebody's telling me in my face I'm lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did not understand me, but let us leave it at that. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If I may add, Your Honour, about the word "lying," in our law system, I had very long discussion with Honourable Judge Bonomy in a previous case about that matter. Because in our country, if you say to someone -- if you say to someone that he's lying, of course, the witness did not understand in the proper way, maybe, maybe, but in our system it's completely different. So I can speak about that hours and hours, and as I said, I had discussion about that issue in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is it different? Explain to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In a court is not allowed to say to someone that he's lying, firstly, in procedure. It is strictly forbidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that's part of your -- that's part of the legal system in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely and very strictly. And one of the worst word if you're going to say to someone is that he is a liar or she is a liar, and even if you find that in a judgement, you know, you're using the word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's precisely opposite in the adversarial system. It's common practice at the end of a cross-examination, such as that which was conducted very vigorously by Mr. Groome, to put to the witness that your whole evidence is nothing but a tissue of lies. That's Mr. Groome's case, and so I was putting it to him, that that is what Mr. Groome was in fact saying, that he's not a witness of truth, but perhaps that is a more sanitized way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You're familiar with it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, I'm completely confident that my witness speaks the truth --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, please speak into the mic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm completely confident about my witness. Hundred per cent confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course. Of course you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But in relation to that issue, I just tried to give some clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I heard that before that in many civil law countries, it's not proper to put to the witness that he's lying. I won't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next -- could we go to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of December, 2008, at 8.50 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.54 a.m.,
